segments.text: Welcome back to Introduction to Machine Learning.
I'm Elutvik Butmann and in this video I will tell you about supervised tasks that we use in machine learning.
You should know at the end the definition and some examples of supervised tasks
and mainly understand the difference between regression and classification.
With supervised tasks we describe data situations where we want to learn the functional relationship
between features and target or between input and output. We have two basic
tasks called regression and classification and whether we are dealing
with regression or classification only depends on the scale of the target
variable. So if the target space is a subspace from R or we have a numerical
target then we are speaking of regression and if the target space is some categorical space
with a finite number of categories then we are speaking of classification.
In statistics the nomenclature here is sometimes a little bit different,
perhaps the term logistic regression. There appears regression but nevertheless it's from
supervised learning prospective classification tasks because we want to differentiate between
two classes. So here are also two examples of a regression and a classification task.
For a regression task on the left hand side we have a numerical target Y and a numerical feature
X, some data points and we try to fit a line to these data points. On the right hand side
for the classification task the target variable is not on the y-axis as on the
left hand side for the regression task but the y label so the target is just
denoted by the symbol and color of these points so we have circles and triangles
and this denotes to which class of the target variable and observation belongs
So here we have two features, x1 and x2, a lot of data points and what we try to
learn is a model that is able to differentiate between these two classes.
So this could be some linear model like here for example a logistic regression
which you will see later but it could also be a nonlinear model and also this
will be treated later. We can, we don't have to, but we can distinguish between
two main reasons to learn this relationship. There's a difference between learning to predict
and learning to explain. In learning to predict we mainly care about the predictive performance
of a model so we really just want to predict very well the target y from some new feature
vector X where we do not know the target Y and an accurate predictor is all we
want. On the other hand in learning to explain we want to understand the
relationship between X and Y or we want to be able to interpret this
relationship or to explain this relationship between X and Y in the data.
Of course, a model that is well able to explain the relationship can also be a good prediction
model, also a good prediction model can be explainable. So these things are not that far
apart. And more or less traditionally, machine learning comes more from the learning to predict
paradigm. And statistics comes more from the learning to explain paradigm. But nowadays,
we really can't make that distinction anymore. Both fields are pursuing
both goals, let's say. Let's finish with three examples on regression and
classification. The first is a regression example where the target variable is the
house price of certain houses and as features we have the size of the house,
number of bedrooms, swimming pool, yes or no. We could want to explain the price
for a certain house. Here in this case we are probably more interested in
learning to explain. We might want to understand what influences a house price
most, but we could also try to make our prediction model to predict if or to
find out if a house is underpriced or not. So learning to explain and learning to
predict could both be viable goals in this example. Second regression example
is the length of stay in in a hospital. So as target variable we have today a
patient stays in the hospital or has stayed in the hospital of course for
historic data and we have features X the diagnosis admission type, gender, age and
others. Also here learning to explain or learning to predict could be helpful.
perhaps the hospital wants to understand which factors drive the length of the stay in the
hospital, to have some policies to perhaps improve their workflows. But on the other hand,
perhaps they just want to predict how long a new patient will be in the hospital to be able to
plan better with their available resources. And as a last example, a classification example,
an insurance in our example the target variable Y is the risk group, perhaps we have five risk
groups for life insurance, customer and we have some features that we might use to predict the risk
of this new customer. So mainly this would be a learning probe to predict but a company might
also be required to explain its predictions to its customers or to some auditing position.
So this also could be learning to predict and learning to explain.
